---
title: "The example study"
---


The package ships a small synthetic study as a regular zotQDA exchange
pair, so every function that reads real exports has something realistic to
read in examples, tests and this documentation:

```r
frag <- qda_read_fragments(qda_example("easyqda-fragments-demo.csv"))
hist <- qda_read_history(qda_example("easyqda-history-demo.csv"))
```

The same two files ship byte-identically in the Python twin
[qdaPy](https://qdapy.zotqda.org)
(`qdapy.example("easyqda-fragments-demo.csv")`), and a test in each package
fails if the copies ever drift apart. Results computed on them are
therefore comparable across the two packages down to the last digit.

Intercoder reliability comes from the **history**, not the fragments. The
fragments file is *last state* — one row per annotation and code, with a
single `codedBy` — so where two coders coded the same segment the last
write wins and the other coder is gone. The per-coder record survives only
in the history, one row per coding event; `qda_codings()` replays its
`add`/`remove` events and `qda_units(coder = "user")` reshapes the result:

```r
u <- qda_units(qda_codings(hist), coder = "user")
qda_agreement(u)
```

Read at the leaf code that gives α = 0.672 and AC1 = 0.674. Flatten the
paths to their top-level theme and the same coders reach α = 0.897 — coders
who split a theme differently still agree on the theme. That gap between
leaf and theme is the **level effect**, and both test suites freeze these
values. Fragments stays for the last-state, corpus-level analyses: code
counts, the code matrix, co-occurrence.

::: {.callout-note title="Synthetic, and saying so"}

Nothing here was ever said by anybody. The interviews, coders and
codings are generated from a fixed random seed, purely so that the
documentation can show real figures and the tests have stable
numbers. Any resemblance to actual studies is the point, not an
accident. But do not cite these numbers as findings.
:::

## What the study is

A fictitious interview study on workload in nursing: eight
semi-structured guide-based interviews, four from a ward (`Station-1` …
`Station-4`) and four from the administration (`Verwaltung-1` …
`Verwaltung-4`). The transcripts follow simple, smoothed rules with
speaker marks (`I:` interviewer, `B:` interviewee); the guide is handled
flexibly, and only the answers are coded. At the disagreement segments both
coders justify their assignment in one name-prefixed comment line each
(`Anna: …` / `Robert: …`) — the same convention the UI uses to attribute
codings to people. Two coders, `Anna` and
`Robert`, coded consensus segments (the same annotations, each with their
own code), following the three-phase method described in the
[zotQDA documentation](https://zotqda.org).

The code system has nine codes in three themes:

| Theme | Codes |
|---|---|
| Belastung | `Zeitdruck`, `emotional`, `körperlich` |
| Ressourcen | `Team`, `Autonomie`, `Anerkennung` |
| Bewältigung | `Humor`, `Distanz`, `Sport` |

## The structure built into it

Each property below exists so that one of the package's analyses has
something true to find:

* **The two settings have different theme profiles.** Burden codes and
  `Ressourcen/Team` dominate the ward, `Autonomie`, `Anerkennung` and
  `Distanz` the administration. This group difference is what
  `qda_ca()` and `qda_code_matrix()` show.
* **Burden and coping travel in pairs.** `emotional`↔`Humor`,
  `Zeitdruck`↔`Distanz`, `körperlich`↔`Sport` and `Team`↔`emotional`
  tend to be coded on the same passage. These co-occurrences are what
  `qda_cluster()` and the scaling map recover.
* **The coders agree often, and disagree systematically.** `Robert` picks
  `Anna`'s code about 78 % of the time; when he differs, it is a
  within-theme neighbour or the partner code, never uniform noise — so
  the confusion table returns a short, interpretable list.
* **Some cells are honest gaps.** `Robert` left about 7 % of the segments
  unrated (`qda_alpha()` handles the gaps), and `Anna` occasionally coded
  a segment twice, so the set-aside count has something to count.
* **The history contains second thoughts.** Six codings were later
  removed; the timeline ignoring them is the documented behaviour.

Positions are present (`positionKind == "text"`) — but because the
segments are consensus segments, both coders carry the same boundaries,
and unitizing measures on this file are trivially high. Measuring
unitizing for real needs each coder's *own* marks, which is a different
export.

## How it was generated

`tool/gen-demo-study.js` in the [zotQDA](https://zotqda.org) repository
writes both files in one run. It builds a native zotQDA model of the study
and drives the plugin's own exporters over it, so the CSVs are a genuine
zotQDA export — produced by the very code that writes a real one, not by a
separate synthesizer. Everything is derived from one fixed seed and fixed
timestamps, with no clock and no environment involved, so the run is
reproducible to the byte, which is what the cross-package identity test
relies on. The column set comes from the exchange contract at run time, so
a contract change shows up here as a regenerated file rather than a stale
one.

The same study also ships inside the plugin as a native, loadable example:
a REFI-QDA project under `examples/pflege-workload`, importable through
zotQDA's project import.

To change the study, edit the constants at the top of that script, run
it once, and update the frozen coefficients in
`tests/testthat/test-demo-export.R` (and qdaPy's
`tests/test_demo_export.py`) to whatever honestly comes out.
